picked.t: Job interview no-shows spark debate over professional etiquette
picked.body: Dinh Minh Quyen, founder of a chain of English-language centers in Bien Hoa, Dong Nai, had scheduled an interview for 3 p.m. early last week. He had already spoken with the candidate by phone and provided details about the position, salary and bonuses, with both sides confirming the appointment. When the candidate had not arrived by 2:58 p.m., Quyen sent a message asking where they were. At 3:01 p.m., the candidate replied that they no longer felt the job was a good fit. Quyen said the candidate, who was under 25 and had relevant expertise, had handled the situation unprofessionally. To make time for the interview, he said he had asked his wife to travel 10 km to take their sick child to hospital. "It’s perfectly normal for a candidate to decide a job is not the right fit. But once an interview has been scheduled, giving advance notice if you need to cancel is simply a matter of respecting the other person’s time," he said. "If you can’t show the basic courtesy of giving advance notice when canceling an appointment, how will you compete in a few years in a job market full of smart technology and candidates who are both capable and considerate?" he asked. His social media post attracted thousands of reactions and quickly divided opinion. Some commenters agreed that failing to show up or cancel beforehand reflected poor communication and could damage a candidate’s professional image. They noted that the candidate had not contacted Quyen proactively and responded only after being asked about the missed appointment. Others argued that Quyen’s family arrangements were his own responsibility and should not be used to criticize the candidate. However, many commenters also pointed out that the candidate had not bothered to cancel himself and only responded only after the CEO sent a message. One comment said: "Not ‘ghosting’ (ignoring) people is basic courtesy. It should not become acceptable behavior simply because ‘all young people are like that these days,’" Many other employers also shared accounts of candidates failing to appear, blocking them or canceling interviews at the last minute. They viewed a candidate’s attitude toward an appointment as an early indication of how that person would work. A candidate’s silence until the last minute showed a lack of respect in communication, a commenter with the handle Hai Anh said. "Professional skills can be taught, but how someone handles an appointment is an early indication of how they work." The debate surrounding Quyen’s story touches on a longstanding issue in the labor market: candidates confirm interviews but then fail to appear or cancel at the last minute. Twenty-three percent of employers had been "ghosted" by candidates after confirming an interview time, a May 2026 survey by recruitment platform CareerLink found. No-shows occurred most frequently during mass recruitment drives, at a rate of 15–20%, Bui Doan Chung, founder of the Nghe Nhan Su Viet Nam (Vietnam Human Resources Profession) platform, said. Workers today have access to information about many jobs at once, and when another opportunity looks more attractive, they change their mind, he said. Ngoc Son, 24, an information technology employee in Hanoi, skipped scheduled interviews at two companies earlier this year. After receiving five interview appointments within a few days, Son attended only two and did not respond to the other companies. He said: "I didn’t know how to respond to them, so I didn’t answer their calls. I thought that if the company couldn’t hire one person, it would call someone else." Chung said a candidate’s absence should not automatically be used as evidence against their character. "In recruitment, a company is essentially selling a job opportunity." To avoid such situations, professional companies now focus on improving their recruitment processes. Automated reminders sent by email, digital calendar, SMS, or phone calls help them know in advance if candidates plan to cancel or reschedule. Many businesses also cancel interviews at the last minute or leave candidates waiting without explanation. CareerLink’s survey found that 58% of companies had, at some point, failed to respond to candidates after interviews. "Candidates have every right to turn down a job opportunity, but how they do so also reflects their professionalism. Respecting other people’s time is, first and foremost, a sign of self-respect," Chung said.

picked.t: Vietnam records nearly 15% rise in foreign tourists as Southeast Asian countries suffer tourism decline
picked.body: Mainland China remained Vietnam's largest source market, with 3.95 million visitors, accounting for about 22.3% of the total. South Korea ranked second with approximately 3.05 million visitors, or 17.3%. Russia ranked third with 1.1 million, followed by Taiwan (964,000) and the U.S. (746,000), according to the General Statistics Office. The rest of the top 10 were Cambodia (688,000), Japan (674,000), India (670,000), the Philippines (522,000) and Australia (485,000). In September, foreign visitors declined by 11.3% from August but rose by 16.5% year-on-year to 1.77 million. Martin Koerner, commercial director of The Anam Group, a chain of luxury resort hotels in Vietnam, said what is particularly encouraging is Vietnam's diversification of source markets. European arrivals increased by more than 50%, while arrivals from markets including the United States, Australia and India also recorded strong growth. This makes Vietnam less dependent on only one or two major Asian source markets, he added. "Vietnam is no longer seen simply as an inexpensive holiday destination. Increasingly, it is being recognized as a destination capable of delivering sophisticated, world-class hospitality," Koerner said. Several Southeast Asian countries have faced declines in international arrivals amid the impact of the Middle East crisis. Thailand received 22.6 million international visitors from January to September, down 3.65% year-on-year, while Singapore recorded 11.43 million in the first eight months, a 1.7% decline from a year earlier. Just over 2 million international tourists visited Cambodia during the first eight months of 2026, down nearly half from the same period last year, The Phnom Penh Post reported.

picked.t: Vietnam has 1,233 ultra-rich individuals, population set for 4th-fastest growth globally
picked.body: The figure was cited at the Personal Financial Planning Forum 2026 in Ho Chi Minh City on Oct. 3 by Chi Huynh, deputy director of the retail banking division at Asia Commercial Bank, Tuoi Tre newspaper reported. Knight Frank’s Wealth Report 2026 forecasts Vietnam’s ultra-high-net-worth population will reach 1,960 by 2031. Only Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and Poland are expected to grow faster, according to Gulf News . Vietnam currently ranks 39th globally by number of people with net assets of at least US$30 million, according to data publisher Visual Capitalist . The expansion reflects a broader rise in financial wealth. Boston Consulting Group expects Vietnam’s financial wealth to grow by more than 9% annually through 2030, among the fastest rates across major emerging markets. Personal financial assets, including cash, deposits, bonds and securities, stood at around US$360 billion at the end of 2022 and could reach about US$600 billion by 2027, according to McKinsey & Company. Nguyen Tien Hoang, dean of finance and banking at Van Lang University, noted that those estimates exclude real estate and gold, which remain major stores of household wealth in Vietnam. He said any shift from those assets into financial products could sharply increase demand for professional wealth management. Industry representatives at the forum said clients are increasingly looking beyond individual products such as deposits, insurance and stocks toward broader financial plans covering different stages of life. Bui Van Huy, CEO of investment advisory firm FIDT, said a more developed wealth management sector could channel household savings into long-term capital for the economy. However, the market still lacks a dedicated legal framework, a broad range of products and common professional standards for advisers, he said. Le Minh Nghia, chairman of the Vietnam Financial Consultants Association, described wealth management as part of the financial market’s "soft infrastructure," rather than a service reserved only for the ultra-rich, Banking Times reported. The forum, now in its fourth year, drew about 500 delegates. Organizers said they plan to submit policy recommendations to regulators on developing a legal framework for wealth management.
